title: Copenhagen to Los Alamos: the Quantum Atom and the Open World
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Ved Stranden: The House of Physiology

stops.name: Copenhagen, Ved Stranden 14 — the birth
stops.campa: Niels Henrik David Bohr is born at Ved Stranden 14, in the house of his mother's family, the Adlers, bankers of Copenhagen, hard against the canal fronting Christiansborg. His father Christian Bohr, professor of physiology at the University, and his mother Ellen, daughter of the Jewish financier David Baruch Adler, raise him and his younger brother Harald in a house full of scientists and disputation. The physiologist's habit of turning every question inside out, testing it relentlessly against the evidence, becomes the boy's own instrument long before he ever touches an equation.
suggested_refs: The commemorative plaque at Ved Stranden 14, unveiled 1960 on Bohr's 75th birthday

stops.name: Copenhagen, the Gammelholm Latin School
stops.campa: At seven Niels enters the Gammelholm Latin School in the old naval quarter, where he and Harald prove indifferent at drawing and composition but formidable at mathematics. Christian Bohr holds open house on Fridays for Copenhagen's ranking minds, the philosopher Harald Høffding among them, and the boys sit at the edge of talk running from Kant to the physiology of respiration. Niels is a slow, deliberate writer even as a child, revising a sentence again and again until it says exactly what he means: the habit that will mark every paper of his life.
suggested_refs: Christian Bohr's Friday gatherings, recalled by Niels and Harald Bohr

stops.name: Copenhagen, the goal at Fælledparken
stops.campa: Grown into a big, strong young man of twenty, Niels keeps goal for Akademisk Boldklub's first team on the common at Fælledparken, while sixteen-year-old Harald plays alongside him at midfield. The brothers are locally known as much for football as for scholarship; three years on, Harald wins Olympic silver with the Danish side in London. Niels is said to lean against the goalpost lost in calculation between shots, trusting his defenders to keep the ball away, and the Copenhagen sporting press remembers the philosopher-goalkeeper long after he has stopped playing.
suggested_refs: Akademisk Boldklub team photographs, 1905-08 seasons
sources: AIP, 'Field Theory: The Soccer Careers of the Bohr Brothers'
Vavel, 'The Bohr Brothers: Football's scholarly siblings'

stops.name: University of Copenhagen, under Christiansen
stops.campa: At the University, Niels comes under Christian Christiansen, Denmark's sole professor of physics, a demanding and original teacher who gives him, almost alone among students, the run of the laboratory. He wins a gold medal of the Royal Danish Academy in 1907 for an experimental study of the vibration of water jets to determine surface tension, working the tables late into the night while Harald checks his prose. In April 1909 he takes his master's degree in physics, already restless with the electron theories of Lorentz and Thomson, sensing gaps neither man will name.
suggested_refs: Bohr's 1907 prize essay on the vibration of water jets, Royal Danish Academy

stops.name: University of Copenhagen, the doctoral defense
stops.campa: On the thirteenth of May Niels defends, in the University's great hall, his doctoral thesis Studies on the Electron Theory of Metals, written — as Danish law then requires — in Danish, so that almost no one outside Scandinavia reads the work that first shows him the electron theories of his day cannot account for magnetism in metals at all. The thesis is a young man's demolition of received authority, Lorentz's electron gas taken apart piece by piece. Denmark has no post that fits his talent yet; a Carlsberg Foundation travel fellowship sends him abroad that autumn, to Cambridge.
suggested_refs: 'Studier over Metallernes Elektrontheori,' Bohr's 1911 doctoral dissertation

segments.name: Cambridge and Manchester: The Quantum Atom

stops.name: Cambridge, the Cavendish Laboratory
stops.campa: Bohr arrives at the Cavendish Laboratory in September to work under J. J. Thomson, discoverer of the electron and reigning authority on the atom's structure — a sphere of positive charge studded with electrons like plums in a pudding. Bohr's English is halting, his manner direct to the point of tactlessness. He carries into Thomson's office his own translated doctoral thesis, open to the page that shows a flaw in Thomson's mathematics, and asks him to read it there and then. Thomson is polite and does not take it up; the collaboration goes nowhere.
suggested_refs: The old Cavendish Laboratory building, Free School Lane, Cambridge

stops.name: Cambridge, the Cavendish Annual Dinner
stops.campa: At the Cavendish's annual dinner Bohr hears the guest of honor speak: Ernest Rutherford, fresh from Manchester, whose gold-foil scattering experiments have just shown, against every pudding model, that an atom is mostly empty space around a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus. Bohr, getting nowhere with Thomson, takes an immediate liking to the blunt, booming New Zealander and resolves on the spot to go to him. It is Rutherford's raw, unfinished nuclear atom, not Thomson's tidy one, that will not let Bohr's mind rest: nothing yet explains why such an atom does not simply collapse.
suggested_refs: The Cavendish Laboratory annual dinner, December 1911

stops.name: Manchester, Rutherford's laboratory
stops.campa: In March Bohr moves to Manchester on Rutherford's invitation, ostensibly to learn radioactive technique, and spends his first weeks measuring the absorption of alpha rays in aluminum foil — competent, unremarkable work. What consumes him is the problem Rutherford's nuclear atom leaves wide open: classical electromagnetism insists an orbiting electron must radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus in an instant, yet atoms plainly endure, and burn with sharp, discrete colors of light rather than a continuous glow. Something outside Maxwell's equations must be holding the atom together and coloring its fire.
suggested_refs: The Victoria University of Manchester physics laboratory, Rutherford's department
sources: University of Manchester, 'Celebrating 100 years of quantum atom discovery'

stops.name: Manchester, the Rutherford memorandum
stops.campa: By June, weeks before he is due home, Bohr drafts for Rutherford a private memorandum sketching, for the first time, electrons confined to fixed rings around the nucleus, their number and arrangement dictating each element's chemistry — the shells that will one day organize the periodic table. He borrows a strange foreign idea, Planck's quantum of action, and forces it onto Rutherford's atom: only certain orbits, he guesses, are allowed at all. Rutherford is encouraging but skeptical of so much built on so little evidence. Bohr returns to Copenhagen in July with the memorandum folded in his notebook, unfinished.
suggested_refs: Bohr's unpublished 'Rutherford memorandum,' June 1912
sources: CERN Courier, 'Rutherford: the road to the nuclear atom'

stops.name: Slagelse, the town hall wedding
stops.campa: On the first of August, having resigned his membership in the Church of Denmark months before, Niels marries Margrethe Nørlund in a civil ceremony at the town hall of Slagelse, her home town. Margrethe becomes his closest collaborator of all: she takes his dictation for nearly every paper of the next fifty years, copies his tortuous revisions clean, and manages the household at the Institute that becomes, in time, a second family for half the physicists of Europe. They honeymoon in England, where Niels cannot resist detouring to show his bride the Manchester laboratory he has just left.
suggested_refs: Slagelse rådhus (town hall), site of the 1912 civil wedding

stops.name: Copenhagen, 'On the Constitution of Atoms and Molecules'
stops.campa: The memorandum becomes, over the winter, three papers under one title, sent to Rutherford in installments and published in the Philosophical Magazine in July, September, and November. Electrons, Bohr proposes, occupy only certain discrete orbits, radiating no energy while they remain in one; light is emitted or absorbed only in the instant an electron leaps between two such orbits, its color fixed by the energy of the jump. The hydrogen spectrum, a puzzle of colored lines unexplained for decades, falls out of the arithmetic exactly. The quantum has entered the atom, which will never again be a miniature solar system.
stops.quote: In order to explain the results of experiments on scattering of alpha rays by matter Prof. Rutherford has given a theory of the structure of atoms... In an attempt to explain some of the properties of matter on the basis of this atom-model we meet, however, with difficulties of a serious nature arising from the apparent instability of the systems of electrons.
stops.quote_source: Niels Bohr, 'On the Constitution of Atoms and Molecules,' Part I, Philosophical Magazine, Series 6, vol. 26 (July 1913)
suggested_refs: Bohr's 1913 trilogy in the Philosophical Magazine, the founding papers of the quantum atom
sources: APS, 'March 6, 1913: Bohr describes his model of atom to Rutherford'

segments.name: Blegdamsvej: The Institute of the New Physics

stops.name: Copenhagen, professor of theoretical physics
stops.campa: The University creates for Bohr, still only thirty, a chair of theoretical physics made to his measure — the first of its kind in Denmark. He begins at once to press the University and the Danish parliament for something no one in Scandinavia yet has: a dedicated institute where theory and experiment share one roof, built for a discipline that barely exists yet as a distinct field. He raises money for years, from the state, the University, and above all the Carlsberg Foundation, the brewer's charitable arm that will underwrite Danish science for the rest of the century.
suggested_refs: Bohr's petition to the Danish parliament for a new institute, 1917-18

stops.name: Copenhagen, Blegdamsvej 17 — the Institute dedicated
stops.campa: In March the University's Institute for Theoretical Physics opens at Blegdamsvej 17, a plain brick building Bohr has shaped down to the seminar room and the ping-pong table in the basement. Within a few years it is simply 'Bohr's Institute,' and within a decade the place every serious young quantum physicist in the world must, at some point, make pilgrimage to: Heisenberg, Pauli, Dirac, Kramers, Klein, Gamow, and Landau pass through its doors to argue, ski with Bohr in Norway, and carry the 'Copenhagen spirit' of merciless, informal debate back to their own countries.
suggested_refs: The Institute for Theoretical Physics, Blegdamsvej 17, renamed the Niels Bohr Institute in 1965
heisenberg.journey.json (shared pin: 'Copenhagen, the Institute on Blegdamsvej')

stops.name: Göttingen, the Bohr-Festspiele
stops.campa: Invited by Max Born and James Franck, Bohr gives a week of lectures at Göttingen that the university half-jokingly calls the Bohr-Festspiele, the Bohr Festival. In the audience, a twenty-year-old doctoral student named Werner Heisenberg stands up and challenges a point in Bohr's own lecture. Most professors would freeze out such a student; Bohr, delighted, invites him to walk on the Hain mountain that afternoon to continue the argument. It is the beginning of the most consequential teacher-student partnership in the physics of the century, and of a friendship a war will later break.
suggested_refs: The Bohr-Festspiele lectures, Göttingen, June 1922
heisenberg.journey.json (shared pin: Heisenberg's first meeting with Bohr)
sources: Heisenberg-Gesellschaft, 'Die Freundschaft zwischen Bohr und Heisenberg'

stops.name: Stockholm, the Nobel lecture
stops.campa: In Stockholm, days after his thirty-seventh birthday, Bohr delivers his Nobel lecture, 'The Structure of the Atom.' Partway through, he departs from his prepared text to announce fresh news just arrived by telegram from his own Institute: element 72, long searched for and long misplaced by chemists among the rare earths, has been found by Dirk Coster and George de Hevesy exactly where Bohr's electron-shell theory said it must be, among the elements resembling zirconium. It will be named hafnium, for Hafnia, the old Latin name of Copenhagen.
suggested_refs: Bohr's Nobel Lecture, 'The Structure of the Atom,' 11 December 1922
sources: Nobel Prize, Bohr Nobel Lecture (11 December 1922)

stops.name: Copenhagen, hafnium confirmed
stops.campa: Through January, Coster and Hevesy confirm the discovery at the Institute with x-ray spectroscopy, the technique that reads an element's atomic number directly off the light its inner electrons emit when struck. The proof completes a chain that began a decade earlier with Bohr's electron shells and Henry Moseley's atomic-number spectra: the periodic table is no longer a list arranged by trial and observation but a structure predicted from first principles, shell by shell, element by element. It is the clearest vindication yet that Bohr's quantum atom, however strange its postulates, describes something true about the world.
suggested_refs: Coster and Hevesy's 1923 hafnium discovery papers

segments.name: Contraria Sunt Complementa: The Debates with Einstein

stops.name: Copenhagen, Heisenberg's uncertainty
stops.campa: While Bohr is away skiing in Norway, Heisenberg, now his assistant at the Institute, works out that position and momentum, or energy and time, cannot both be measured to unlimited precision at once: to fix one is, in the nature of things, to blur the other. Bohr returns and pushes back hard on Heisenberg's reasoning, though not his conclusion, driving him near tears in argument before the two agree the uncertainty is real but rests on something deeper: not merely a clumsiness of measurement, but the impossibility of separating the observed system from the act of observing it.
suggested_refs: Heisenberg's uncertainty principle paper, 1927
heisenberg.journey.json (shared pin: 'Copenhagen, the paper while Bohr is skiing')

stops.name: Como, the Volta Conference
stops.campa: At Lake Como, in a conference marking the centenary of Alessandro Volta's death, Bohr gives the lecture 'The Quantum Postulate and the Recent Development of Atomic Theory,' publicly naming for the first time the principle he calls complementarity: wave and particle, position and momentum, are not contradictory pictures of the electron but complementary ones, each valid, neither complete alone, and never simultaneously exact. Nature herself, he argues, forces the choice of one experimental arrangement or another, and with it, one description or the other. Einstein is absent from Como; he will meet the idea head-on the following month, at Brussels.
suggested_refs: Bohr's Como lecture, 'The Quantum Postulate,' September 1927

stops.name: Brussels, the Fifth Solvay Conference
stops.campa: At the Institut de Physiologie Solvay in Brussels, the world's foremost physicists gather, and the argument that will define the rest of both men's lives begins in earnest between Bohr and Einstein. Over breakfast Einstein invents a thought experiment meant to show quantum mechanics incomplete; by dinner Bohr has found the flaw, often turning Einstein's own physics against him. Einstein, unconvinced that nature is at bottom a matter of probabilities, writes to Max Born around this time that he is convinced God does not play dice with the universe.
suggested_refs: The 1927 Solvay Conference photograph, seventeen Nobel laureates
einstein.journey.json (shared pin: 'Brussels, the debates with Bohr')
sources: Aeon, 'What Einstein meant by God does not play dice'
arXiv, 'Quantum Theory at the Crossroads: the 1927 Solvay Conference'

stops.name: Brussels, the Sixth Solvay Conference — the photon box
stops.campa: Three years on, at the Sixth Solvay Conference, Einstein returns with his most ingenious challenge yet: a box leaking a single photon at a precisely timed instant, weighed before and after on a spring scale, so both the photon's energy and the moment of its escape might be known exactly, defeating the uncertainty principle outright. Bohr is reportedly stricken through the night, unable to find the error, until by morning he has it: weighing the box, Einstein's own general relativity shows, introduces an uncertainty in its position, and so in the flow of time inside it, that restores the very balance Einstein sought to break.
suggested_refs: The photon-box thought experiment, Sixth Solvay Conference, 1930
sources: ar5iv, 'Complementarity in the Bohr-Einstein Photon Box'

stops.name: Copenhagen, the Institute as refuge
stops.campa: As the new German government dismisses Jewish and politically suspect scientists from their posts through 1933, Bohr and his Institute become a clearinghouse for refuge: he raises money through the Danish Rockefeller committee and his own reputation to place displaced physicists and chemists across Europe, America, and Palestine, corresponding tirelessly on their behalf and often housing them at Blegdamsvej while arrangements are made. James Franck, Otto Frisch, and dozens of others owe a debt to this quiet, unglamorous labor, carried on alongside his physics, in the years before the Institute's own doors will need defending.
suggested_refs: The Danish committee for the support of refugee intellectual workers, 1933

stops.name: The Sound, off north Zealand — Christian's drowning
stops.campa: Sailing with his father and friends off the coast of Zealand, Christian, Niels and Margrethe's eldest son and, by every account, the most gifted of their six boys, is swept overboard when a sudden squall strikes the boat, and drowns before he can be reached. Niels, who has weathered every argument of Einstein's without visible strain, is broken by this in a way colleagues never see him broken by physics; he speaks of the accident rarely, and always with the particular, exact grief of a father who watched and could not act in time. Aage, Hans, Erik, and Ernest remain; Aage will one day share his father's Nobel Prize.
suggested_refs: The Bohr family sailing accident, summer 1934

stops.name: Princeton and Washington — the news of fission
stops.campa: Bohr arrives in New York on the sixteenth of January carrying, from Otto Frisch and Lise Meitner in Copenhagen, news he can barely contain: uranium bombarded by neutrons has been shown to split, fission, releasing energy on a scale no chemical reaction approaches. At Princeton he and John Wheeler work out which uranium isotope fissions and why; on the twenty-sixth, at the Fifth Washington Conference on Theoretical Physics, Bohr and Enrico Fermi announce the discovery to American physicists. Word that a chain reaction, and conceivably a weapon, might follow spreads through the community within days.
suggested_refs: The Fifth Washington Conference on Theoretical Physics, George Washington University, January 1939
sources: Physics Today, 'Bringing the News of Fission to America'

stops.name: Copenhagen, the German invasion
stops.campa: German troops cross the border before dawn, and Denmark, informed it cannot resist, surrenders within hours to preserve what it can of its institutions and its king. Bohr, half-Jewish through his mother, chooses to stay at his post rather than flee, believing the Institute's continued, visible operation under occupation is itself a form of resistance, and that his presence may shield colleagues and students. He refuses all approaches from German physicists to leave for safer, more prestigious work abroad, and refuses equally any collaboration with the occupying administration.
suggested_refs: The German occupation of Denmark, 9 April 1940
sources: Defense Media Network, 'The Rescue of Danish Jews'

stops.name: Copenhagen, the gold dissolved
stops.campa: With the invasion under way, Bohr and the Hungarian chemist George de Hevesy face an urgent problem: the gold Nobel medals of Max von Laue and James Franck, sent to Copenhagen for safekeeping from Germany, must not fall into Nazi hands as evidence of dissent, nor be found and confiscated as gold. Hevesy dissolves both medals in aqua regia, nitric and hydrochloric acid together, and leaves the innocuous orange liquid on a shelf among hundreds of other bottles in the Institute. German soldiers search the building without a second glance at it; after the war the gold is recovered from solution and the medals recast.
suggested_refs: The beaker of dissolved Nobel gold, Institute for Theoretical Physics

stops.name: Copenhagen, the Carlsberg mansion — Heisenberg's visit
stops.campa: Heisenberg, now head of the German nuclear program, comes to Copenhagen for a German cultural institute's symposium and, three times, to Bohr's home at the Carlsberg mansion, ostensibly to see his old teacher again. On one visit, walking together to avoid microphones, he raises the subject of atomic weapons; what exactly he says, and what he means by it, Bohr and Heisenberg will remember so differently for the rest of their lives that the conversation becomes one of the century's great unresolved mysteries. Bohr comes away convinced, rightly or not, that Germany is racing to build the bomb, and that his former student is helping.
suggested_refs: The Niels Bohr Archive's released Bohr-Heisenberg documents (2002)
heisenberg.journey.json (shared pin: 'Copenhagen, the visit to Bohr')
sources: Defense Media Network, 'The Copenhagen Meeting of Heisenberg and Bohr'

stops.name: Copenhagen, the flight begins
stops.campa: Word reaches the Danish resistance, and through them Bohr, that the Gestapo plans his arrest within days, alongside the roundup of Danish Jews already being prepared for the first of October. Bohr had resisted leaving for three years of occupation; he does not resist now. On the night of the twenty-ninth he and Margrethe are smuggled from the Carlsberg mansion by resistance fighters, crossing to the coast in secrecy and out onto a small fishing boat bound across the Sound for neutral Sweden, leaving behind the Institute, the medals in their bottle, and almost everything else.
suggested_refs: The Danish resistance escape network across the Øresund, autumn 1943
sources: timboyce.com, '1943 — Niels Bohr and wife escape from Denmark to Sweden'
Lindau Nobel, 'Bohr & Heisenberg: Two Physicists in Occupied Copenhagen'

stops.name: Limhamn, Sweden — landfall
stops.campa: The fishing boat makes the Swedish coast near Limhamn safely, and Bohr, fifty-seven years old, sets foot as a refugee on neutral ground for the first time in his life. German agents in Stockholm, alerted to his flight, discuss whether he might yet be seized or killed before he can reach Britain; Swedish authorities move him quickly and quietly toward the capital. He carries almost nothing of value from Copenhagen — a beer bottle he grabbed in the dark, believing it held heavy water smuggled from the Institute, turns out on inspection to hold nothing more than beer.
suggested_refs: The crossing point near Limhamn, Öresund, September 1943
sources: Defense Media Network, 'The Rescue of Danish Jews'
TWZ, 'The Nuclear Scientist And The Warplane'

stops.name: Stockholm, before King Gustav V
stops.campa: In Stockholm Bohr refuses to leave for Britain, or to rest, until Sweden commits itself publicly: he tells officials, and finally the King himself, that he will not go until the government announces over the airwaves and in the press that its border stands open to Denmark's Jews. On the second of October, Gustav V makes the announcement Bohr has pressed for, and the Danish resistance, already ferrying refugees across the Sound in secret, gains the one thing it lacked: a guaranteed welcome on the far shore. In three weeks nearly all of Denmark's Jewish population, some eight thousand people, crosses to safety.
suggested_refs: King Gustav V's public announcement of asylum, 2 October 1943
The rescue of the Danish Jews, October 1943
sources: Guttermans, 'The Amazing Story of the Danish Rescue'

stops.name: Bromma Airport — the Mosquito flight
stops.campa: At Bromma, ground crew of a British Overseas Airways Mosquito, its bomb bay refitted as a cramped passenger space for exactly this kind of extraction, seal Bohr inside with flares, a parachute, and an oxygen mask he is briefed on but does not properly use. Over the North Sea, at altitude, he loses consciousness from lack of oxygen; the pilot, guessing from his silence on the intercom that something is wrong, descends until he revives. Bohr lands in Scotland, and within days is in London, inducted into the secret of the Anglo-American bomb project.
suggested_refs: BOAC Mosquito FB.VI G-AGGG, the aircraft that carried Bohr, 6 October 1943
sources: TWZ, 'The Nuclear Scientist And The Warplane That Became Britain's Most Unlikely Airliner'
Warrior Maven, 'Niels Bohr's Flight From the Nazis Was a Science Drama'

stops.name: Washington, arrival under an alias
stops.campa: In December Bohr and his son Aage, a young physicist in his own right, arrive in the United States to join the British scientific mission to the Manhattan Project, traveling and working under the assumed names Nicholas and James Baker so that neutral Sweden's press cannot report that the world's most famous physicist has surfaced in America. The alias fools almost no one who meets him — Bohr's face and manner are unmistakable — but it serves its bureaucratic purpose, and 'Uncle Nick' becomes the affectionate name colleagues use for him for the rest of the war.
suggested_refs: Bohr's British mission travel papers under the alias 'Nicholas Baker'
robert_oppenheimer.journey.json (shared pin: Bohr on the mesa)
sources: ladailypost.com, 'Nobel Laureate Niels Bohr Brought Winter Cheer To Los Alamos'

stops.name: Los Alamos — 'is it big enough?'
stops.campa: At the secret mesa-top laboratory built to design the bomb itself, Bohr arrives as elder statesman rather than day-to-day worker, and the mesa reveres him like a prophet. He asks Oppenheimer the question that reframes the whole endeavor: is the weapon big enough, big enough not merely to win a war but to end all war, by forcing the nations into an openness they would never otherwise choose? He preaches the open world and the international control that must follow such a weapon; Oppenheimer takes the idea into himself, and it becomes his own postwar gospel.
suggested_refs: robert_oppenheimer.journey.json (shared pin: 'Bohr on the mesa: is it big enough?')
sources: blog.nuclearsecrecy.com, 'What did Bohr do at Los Alamos?'

stops.name: London, the meeting with Churchill
stops.campa: Convinced the bomb's existence must be disclosed to the Soviet Union before the war ends, to forestall a secret postwar arms race rather than provoke one, Bohr secures an audience with Churchill through his friend Lord Cherwell. The meeting goes badly from the first minute: Churchill, suspicious and impatient, treats Bohr's careful argument as naive interference in matters of state, and the two talk past each other for the whole half hour. Bohr leaves shaken, and tells colleagues afterward what the encounter felt like.
stops.quote: It was terrible. He treated us like two schoolboys.
stops.quote_source: Bohr, recalled to colleagues after the meeting, quoted in Jacques Hymans, 'Churchill and Hiroshima,' London Review of Books blog (2015)
suggested_refs: Bohr's 16 May 1944 audience with Churchill, arranged via Lord Cherwell
sources: International Churchill Society, 'The Bomb and the Special Relationship'

stops.name: Washington, the White House — Roosevelt
stops.campa: Where Churchill dismissed him, Roosevelt receives Bohr courteously at the White House and listens through a long conversation grounded in the memorandum Bohr submitted weeks before: that the bomb's existence be shared with the Allies, the Soviet Union included, before it is used, in exchange for a binding international system of control, forestalling the arms race Bohr believes otherwise inevitable. Roosevelt seems sympathetic, even receptive, and Bohr leaves hopeful his proposal has found a hearing at the highest level. The hope does not survive the month.
stops.quote: It certainly surpasses the imagination of anyone to survey the consequences of the project in years to come... a weapon of an unparalleled power is being created which will completely change all future conditions of warfare.
stops.quote_source: Bohr, memorandum to President Roosevelt, 3 July 1944, quoted in Bohr's Open Letter to the United Nations, 9 June 1950
suggested_refs: Bohr's memorandum to President Roosevelt, 3 July 1944
sources: AHF, 'Niels Bohr's Memorandum to President Roosevelt'
Bohr, Open Letter to the United Nations (1950)

stops.name: Hyde Park, New York — the Aide-Mémoire
stops.campa: At Roosevelt's Hyde Park estate, meeting privately after the Quebec Conference, Churchill and Roosevelt reject Bohr's proposal outright and go further: they initial an aide-mémoire agreeing the bomb's existence must remain secret until used, possibly against Japan, and that Bohr himself should be watched, his contacts investigated, to ensure he leaks nothing, particularly to the Russians, whom he has never in fact approached. Bohr is not told of the document and does not learn of its harsher clauses for years; he believes, wrongly, that his warning has simply gone unheeded rather than been actively suppressed.
suggested_refs: The Hyde Park Aide-Mémoire, 19 September 1944

stops.name: Los Alamos, the initiator
stops.campa: Back at Los Alamos through the winter, Bohr turns to a stubborn engineering puzzle at the heart of the plutonium bomb: the initiator, a device that must release a precise burst of neutrons at exactly the right instant to start the chain reaction cleanly. Where the project's younger physicists have circled the problem for months, Bohr, working through it with Oppenheimer and others in early February, clarifies the physics needed to solve it. It is his last substantial technical contribution to the weapon whose political consequences will occupy the rest of his life.
stops.quote: This device remained a stubborn puzzle, but in early February 1945, Niels Bohr clarified what had to be done.
stops.quote_source: J. Robert Oppenheimer, quoted in blog.nuclearsecrecy.com, 'What did Bohr do at Los Alamos?'
suggested_refs: The plutonium bomb's neutron initiator, solved February 1945
sources: blog.nuclearsecrecy.com, 'What did Bohr do at Los Alamos?'

stops.name: Copenhagen, the return home
stops.campa: With the war in Europe over, Bohr and Margrethe return to Copenhagen and the Institute at Blegdamsvej, found largely intact: the bottle of dissolved gold still on its shelf, waiting to be recovered and recast into the Nobel medals of Franck and von Laue. Bohr resumes the directorship he has held for over two decades, rebuilding the international traffic of young physicists the war interrupted, and turns the moral weight of his wartime experience toward a single, sustained public argument: that the secrecy surrounding atomic weapons is itself the deepest danger the world now faces.
suggested_refs: The recasting of the Franck and von Laue Nobel medals, postwar

stops.name: Copenhagen, the coat of arms
stops.campa: Made a Knight of the Order of the Elephant by King Frederik IX in recognition of his life's work, Bohr must, by the order's custom, design his own coat of arms. At the suggestion of Hannah Rozental, a scholar of Chinese thought, he chooses for its central field the ancient taijitu, the interlocking curves of yin and yang, and sets beneath it a motto of his own coinage: contraria sunt complementa, opposites are complementary. It is complementarity itself, first named at Como twenty years before, carried now into heraldry: the wave is not the enemy of the particle, nor is either alone the whole truth.
stops.quote_source: Motto of Bohr's coat of arms, granted on his knighthood in the Order of the Elephant, 17 October 1947
suggested_refs: Niels Bohr's coat of arms, designed 1947, taijitu and Latin motto
sources: Renaissance Universal, 'Niels Bohr's fascination with Yin and Yang'

stops.name: New York, the Open Letter to the United Nations
stops.campa: From Copenhagen, Bohr addresses an open letter to the United Nations, laying out publicly, for the first time, the arguments he had pressed privately on Roosevelt and Churchill during the war: that only complete openness between nations, the free exchange of scientific and industrial information across every border, can prevent the atomic age from ending in catastrophe. Secrecy bred of mutual distrust is now, he argues, the graver danger, greater than any single weapon. He does not expect the great powers to act on it soon; he means the letter as a marker, voiced publicly so it cannot simply be forgotten.
stops.quote: An open world where each nation can assert itself solely by the extent to which it can contribute to the common culture and is able to help others with experience and resources must be the goal to be put above everything else.
stops.quote_source: Niels Bohr, Open Letter to the United Nations, 9 June 1950
suggested_refs: Bohr's Open Letter to the United Nations, 9 June 1950, full text
sources: Bohr, Open Letter to the United Nations (9 June 1950), fredsakademiet.dk

stops.name: Copenhagen, the founding of CERN
stops.campa: Bohr lends his name, his diplomacy, and for several years his own Institute's spare rooms to the founding of CERN, the European Council for Nuclear Research, a project he sees as science's own small working model of the open world he has argued for: nations pooling resources and information rather than hoarding them behind military secrecy. Before the Geneva laboratory is built, CERN's first theoretical study division operates out of Blegdamsvej itself, a fitting home for an institution founded on the premise that fundamental physics is safest, and best, done in the open and in common.

stops.name: Washington, the Atoms for Peace Award
stops.campa: At the National Academy of Sciences in Washington, President Eisenhower presents Bohr with the first Atoms for Peace Award, honoring both his physics and the postwar campaign for openness his Open Letter began. It is, in effect, the world's official answer, seven years late and only partial, to what Bohr asked of the United Nations in 1950: not the full transparency he wanted, but at least public acknowledgment that the argument was the right one to have made. Bohr, seventy-two, accepts it as a working physicist still, not yet a monument to himself.
suggested_refs: The first Atoms for Peace Award medal, presented 24 October 1957
sources: Physics Today, 'Bohr Wins Atoms for Peace Prize'

stops.name: Copenhagen, the Carlsberg mansion — the death
stops.campa: Bohr dies of heart failure at the Æresbolig, the honorary residence at Carlsberg the Royal Danish Academy granted him in 1931, in the house where he has lived and worked for over thirty years. He had given, only days before, an extended interview on his life and the history of quantum theory, and colleagues find, still on the blackboard of his study, an unfinished sketch he had drawn: the diagram of Einstein's photon-box experiment, the old argument from Brussels in 1930, worked over one more time as though the last word on complementarity had still not quite been said.
suggested_refs: The blackboard sketch of Einstein's photon box, found in Bohr's study, 18 November 1962
